segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, a subject close to all of our hearts, food, and in particular, the politics of food.
It was a discussion I chaired at this year's Sydney Writers Festival. And before we got going, I was fascinated to know what the audience's attitudes were to food.
And I found that most of them were on a gluten-free diet and a large proportion were watching their carbs.
Anyway, on the panel were Indira Naidoo, author of The Oedipal Balcony and The Edible City,
Damon Gamow, author of That Sugar Book and producer and host of That Sugar Film,
and Julian Baggini, a British philosopher and prolific writer,
including The Virtues of the Table and The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten.
What do you think about people being food-focused, Julian?
You've got strong opinions about that.
Well, do I? I have strong opinions.
Well, you wrote a book about it.
Yeah, I did write a book about it, yeah.
My philosophical influences are people like Aristotle and David Hume, who actually had very little to say about food.
But if you go to Aristotle, Aristotle advocated this doctrine of the mean, which is actually, funnily enough, Confucius also advocated something similar.
And that kind of way of looking at things says that, generally speaking, extremist positions tend to be wrong, and the appropriate thing is something in between.
Now I think the Western philosophical tradition has tended to be sort of really down on food and on the body
And tend to think that anyone who pays any attention to it at all is kind of deluded
You know, they're just like animals because that's what animals eat
So if you focus on eating you're like an animal
Briat Savarin the French food writer said, you know, animals feed and humans eat
Food is a very important part of life. It's part of what makes us human
It's very humanizing and it connects us to all sorts of important issues. At the same time though to become obsessive about food
There are certain food obsessions I think are legitimate.
If you're a really creative chef, for example,
or you're a really great producer of food, that's your obsession.
But there are unhealthy obsessions around food, for sure.
So it's about finding the appropriate balance for it in life,
the appropriate place for it, which is neither everything nor nothing.
No, the Edible City is all about bringing people together around food, isn't it?
Yes, it is.
And I'm certainly of the school of thought.
The first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning is what I'm going to eat,
and the last thing I think about is what I'm going to eat the next day.
And in between times?
Is there any time you don't think about food?
I tend to eat about two or three times a day.
But for me, food is much more than a really important part of our life.
One of the tragedies we've fallen into in the Western modern way of looking at food
is that it's something we've developed these paranoias about.
Oh my God, what is that going to do to me if I eat that?
And so that's been really concerning because for me,
it's a joyous experience.
You know, food is joyous to eat.
The anticipation of food, the sharing of food,
the actual process of eating it,
and then the discussion around it.
So for me, it's a sad day
when food isn't the central part of a day.
And I think that that's where it's become really disturbing
is that it's this also-ran thing,
this thing I just pick up on the way
or pull out of a packet
or pull something out of a tin or a container.
I think that that's where the problems have become,
that we've reduced food rather than elevate it to where it should be.
We certainly have reduced food, but do you think Damon has reduced food
and created all sorts of paranoia through his best-selling books?
You can answer honestly, it's fine.
No, do you think so?
Look, I think in terms of Damon's work and Damon's book,
obviously I'm very concerned about the amount of sugar in our diets
and I think that it is a big problem.
You know, we're eating something like, I think, 1,000% more sugar than we did 200 years ago.
It's leading to lots of disease and wellness issues.
What are you going to do about your dessert menus if you abandon food?
Well, I think that we went through the stage when we demonised fat.
We went through the stage when we demonised protein.
And I think that we have to be aware that there are some things we need to have in moderation, like sugar.
But you can't look at food in terms of just its nutrients.
You have to look at it holistically.
look at the apple, not just look at it as a sum of proteins and nutrients and fats and sugars.
And I think that that's where we're going a little wrong.
So, Damon, I've got a bone to pick with you.
Pick away.
Last night, I tried one of your recipes.
So I'm to blame.
I almost sliced my finger chopping broccoli.
You need to improve your culinary skills.
I do.
I find that technique.
Were you surprised by the polling of the audience in terms of the food obsessions in the audience or food interest?
Well, I think we've got to be very careful.
I think what we're in the middle of at the moment is the food revolution,
where people are starting to empower themselves with information about food.
And I don't necessarily think that's a bad thing.
As long as it stays in a sort of safe area,
I think we've been misled for 35 years in a lot of different ways.
I think the environment has supported companies making enormous amounts of profit,
telling us what to eat,
and shaping their marketing strategies to get us hooked on these kind of products.
And certainly where I come from is that we don't think sugar per se is bad
or evil, we're trying to get people to say, look, the World Health Organisation recommends
about six teaspoons of sugar a day. Our teenagers are having about 40 teaspoons. So clearly there's
a lack of understanding with the food supply. So how do we teach people those skills to
raise their awareness, learn to read labels, understand what they're putting in their bodies?
Because I think now the science tells us not only the physical symptoms, but your mental,
your vitality, your emotions are determined by the foods you're eating. And if we can get
this through to kids, we're going to set them up for a much healthier lifestyle. That's
not to say that we demonise these foods, we just get them to take responsibility and understand
what they're putting in their bodies. So do you think that you can actually counter the effect
of the globalised food industry? Well I think we're going to have to because you know the reality is
what we're using nearly 40% of our land now for farming, we're going to be 9 billion people by
2050. We need to rethink the way we approach food and I think that's going to switch us back to
local. We're going to have to teach kids about growing their own vegetables because we can't
keep going the way we are. So we need people to understand food a bit more. And I think the key
with sugar is that we forget that sugar is not a nutrient. There is no biological requirement for
added sugar in our diet. We can get all the sugar we need from fruits and vegetables and other
sources. So as a treat, fantastic every now and again. But we've got to a point where it's now
in 80% of the food supply and most people are having 30 or 40 teaspoons a day. That's not a
treat anymore. That's kind of tipped the balance and that's why we're seeing this catastrophic
health crisis. True. Yeah, because it's only the food industry, because I think sometimes
the food industry is presented as this huge, big, all-powerful demon which exerts huge
control over us. And of course, there have been abuses. Damon's film points to the way
in which there's been some misinformation and deliberate suppression of information
about the health of food. So clearly, I'm not saying they're blameless, but I think
that the danger of putting that kind of view of the food industry is it makes it seem like
we're less powerful than we are. And also, we've got to remember, at the end of the day,
they are about making money, right? At the end of the day, it's consumer demand. When
When the consumers start demanding organic, they stock the organic.
When they want reduced sugar, they stock reduced sugar.
So they're not going to foist these things upon us if we don't willingly take them.
With more information, we make our choices, the food industry will respond.
But isn't that a bit naive?
Because what we have is a saturated fat mountain, we have a sugar mountain.
All the food that people don't eat gets put into a mountain and then put into high-calorie,
low-value foods.
there is a degree of dumping and creation of markets too.
Well, there is, but remember,
people aren't entirely powerless about that,
except, and this is where it gets very interesting,
the politics, of course, where people are poor,
where there's not enough money, right?
So I think in developed countries,
most people actually have the resources
to eat proper good food.
It's often not more expensive if you know where to get it,
but let's be honest, generally speaking,
you do have to pay a bit to get the quality stuff.
Most people can afford that.
They choose other priorities.
It's as simple as that.
But there's always that 10, 20% of people
in countries like Australia and in Britain who have very little money.
And those are the people who have very little choice
but to buy those processed products with all these things in it.
So that's where the politics, I think, gets more tricky.
I agree with Julian in terms of the food companies do respond to consumers.
I mean, in the end, they're there to make money.
And if consumers want a particular product with a particular composition,
they will respond to it.
I mean, we have seen examples of that here in Australia.
My concern is when consumers show that they want a certain product,
for instance, we're having a big debate in Australia at the moment
with our free-range eggs.
Now, consumers have shown that they want free-range eggs,
but they want them to be labelled accurately.
And unfortunately, the policy makers aren't helping consumers
make that decision.
So eggs are being labelled as free-range when they're...
Just in a larger cage.
Exactly.
10,000 chickens to a shed instead of the 1,500, which is the code.
Now, this makes it really hard for consumers.
They want to do the right thing.
They want to buy free range,
but they're presented with a product that clearly is not.
And what that does is the people who are doing the right thing,
the egg farmers who are doing the right thing,
looking after those animals well
and delivering a free range product,
are getting messed up in the caged hens
and the limited access to outdoor pasture.
So that's why, for me, it needs to be a two-pronged approach.
Consumers, yes, say,
we've now got the information this is what we want.
if the companies say, OK, we'll respond to that.
But the policymakers have to make sure that those regulations are enforced
and the people who do the wrong thing are punished.
And the problem in Australia that we found with the film
is that we've had two UK parliamentary screenings,
New Zealand parliamentary screening.
We had two scheduled in Australia and not one politician turned up,
didn't even send an intern.
And I got to go and meet one of the ministers
and we're the second biggest exporter of sugar in the world.
So it's a kind of a don't-go-there topic.
And at the same time, look, there are a host of factors that are contributing to the diseases we're seeing,
but sugar is a major factor, especially around kids, that if they had the gumption to actually take some...
I agree, it's part empowering the consumer, but also the government need to help out in some way,
whether it's regulating the companies, but they need to take action.
So it's been said that big food is acting like big tobacco now.
One of the things that we know works with tobacco, and particularly in children, is price.
Where do you stand on a sugar tax?
Well, I guess the only working model of it so far has come out of Mexico,
and it's now been 18 months.
They put a levy on sugary drinks.
They've seen a 17% reduction in their lower socioeconomic areas.
But more importantly, they've raised $1.8 billion.
So the only way I would support it,
and I don't think this is going to happen,
is if we set up a transparent, independent body that said,
all right, with that money raised, we're going to actively...
So I'd complicate it into...
That's it. Let's use it to subsidise fresh fruits and vegetables.
Let's revamp our hospital system and our schools
and gave them fresh, affordable foods.
But unfortunately, I don't think we're going to see that happen.
It's going to disappear into the coffers.
A new submarine in South Australia.
There you go.
But then people say it's the nanny state.
People have got control over their lives, Julian.
Let it be.
Nanny state arguments are very easy to make.
The fact of the matter is that we support regulation of all sorts of things for our mutual benefit.
It's not a nanny because if the restrictions are there with the consent and the approval and the demand of the populace,
it's something we choose together, right?
It's not about the state saying, you can't do that.
But also, I think the other problem with the nanny state argument is we've got to remember that the people who make that case,
imagine that there's something out there which is called the pure free market,
which is operating independently of any government on policy issues, and that that is sufficient.
That is not the case, and it never has been the case.
We have the kind of foods we have, in the proportion we have them, at the price we have them,
for all sorts of very complicated issues around agricultural subsidy,
trade tariffs and so forth.
The food supply system is saturated in policy and law and regulation.
So when someone says,
what we're going to do is we want to change a part of that
to get slightly better results,
you're not introducing an interventionism which wasn't there before.
You're simply changing what exactly is being intervened about.
So it's perfectly legitimate.
Yeah, I agree, absolutely.
We do tend to forget that government policy has led us to where we are in our food system
at the moment.
I mean, it hasn't happened separate to government policy.
They've been actively intervening in that process over the last 10, 20, 30 years.
And also, too, you've got to remember that the food companies are actively intervening
as well.
Every couple of months, they're changing compositions of foods to amp up sugar, amp
up salt or fat.
So the whole system, it's not that you're just being given a product that just sits
there and hasn't been changed in a number of decades. Everyone involved in this process
is changing compositions. And we've unfortunately, in terms of government policy and health policy,
been lagging behind. We've not been keeping up with how willing big business is to change the
composition of foods to make it almost impossible not to be addictive. I mean, our brains love salt,
fat and sugar. I mean, who in this room doesn't love that? You're listening to a discussion on
the politics of food from this year's Sydney Writers' Festival. On the panel are Indira Naidoo,
Damon Gamow, and philosopher Julian Bajini. I want to get back to a comment that Damon made
right at the beginning, which is, you know, a back-to-the-earth idea of growing your own food,
which you give, I think, four examples in the edible city, a couple in Melbourne and Sydney,
Wayside Chapel and so on. But to what extent is it scalable? We're trying to limit the size of our
cities, lose the quarter-eater block, live in apartments. I know you've got the balcony idea,
but nonetheless, how practical is it that we can get back in touch with our food?
I think we really need to. We've all become grossly disconnected from our food. And the
groups I particularly work with are the ones that are suffering most from this new food world. You
know, they're poor, disadvantaged, homeless, newly arrived immigrants, asylum seekers, elderly,
retired, kids in school. So they're the people, unfortunately, that so many of these bad
products are being directed at. And what I've found from my work is when you help these communities
reconnect with their food, even if it's just growing a few pots of herbs on their balcony
or on the stairwell or if they have a balcony or a little garden, that process of seeing how
something grows, to see a piece of fruit, to see a lettuce, a cabbage, an apple actually grow,
has been quite transformative for so many of these communities because, you know, something like 60%
But in the end, it's cheaper to buy something from the burger shop down the road.
Well, you have to educate people about what cheap actually means.
And I think that we've gone through an era where we expect food to be cheap.
But what we don't understand is that so many of the external costs of that food
haven't actually been priced into the cost of that food.
So that apple...
So the food miles, the transportation.
So a McDonald's hamburger may cost $3.
But when you look at the food miles, the environmental aspect,
the low wages paid to workers, the cost of pollution, whatever it might be,
if you really put all those costs into the value for hamburger,
actually the average person probably wouldn't be able to afford it.
And when you...
But isn't that slightly naive?
Because you should have it costed into the price of the hamburger, but it's not.
And if you haven't got much money, then that's what your money goes on.
Absolutely.
I mean, I'm not someone who's anti-hamburgers particularly,
but it's about what you help people get access to.
And in the suburbs I work in, sometimes fast food is the only thing they have.
There's no grocery stores, not even a general supermarket.
So you have to work within that.
But once you introduce that sense that they can have a little bit of autonomy,
see how food grows, what it takes to grow food,
it starts making them think differently.
So when you buy an eggplant for five cents or ten cents at the supermarket
and it's taken you three months to grow it,
you ask different questions as a conscious consumer and eater
than you would have as just a consumer.
And I think that that is part of the process.
Obviously, no one is going to be able to grow all the food they need when you live in urban
environments and cities, but we can certainly grow much more of our food.
We can localise it much more, make it more nutritious and more accessible and also cheaper.
You know, our homeless community in the Wayside Chapel in Potts Point I work with, 200 square
metres on our rooftop, we grow vegetables.
We have five or six beehives producing honey.
and when our homeless visitors arrive in the garden
every Thursday for garden class,
the first thing they do is literally eat the garden.
That is their meal for the day.
And when the first time that happened,
it really blew me away
because obviously they don't have the income
to buy nutritious food
and for them, that vegetable garden is their supermarket.
So how to do these adjustments, Damon?
I kind of agree with Indira in the sense
that we're not going to have a choice.
I think we're going to have to switch
to this kind of micro-farming food towers.
we're going to have to start growing more local.
And the World Watch Institute did a report that said
that 80% of New York residents could be fed from rooftop gardens.
And the way we're heading, the impact on our food now,
apples being shipped from London to South Africa to be polished
and then shipped back to the UK to be sold.
I mean, it's absolutely mad.
We need to find a way to promote local eating again.
And I think, as Indira was saying,
I think a burger should be reflective of what its true value is
in terms of those miles.
So if you want a hamburger, great, but it's going to be $11.
But if you want the local banana, it's going to be 40 cents
because it's down the road.
So that implies differential taxation by governments?
Well, I think it's inevitable.
I think we don't realise the impact of what's happening to our climate.
I don't think it's...
People don't understand how food's going to be affected
in the next 40 or 50 years.
We are going to have to make some fundamental decisions around that
because we cannot keep going the way we are.
So I think the more we can force people to try and grow their own,
have these community gardens, it's going to help.
Yeah, I mean, I've got reservations about all of this.
I think that it's always good to grow food for various reasons,
not mainly around self-sufficiency, I would say, actually,
to do with other things, connection and stuff.
but I think there's a bit of a danger of kind of turning this local thing into a kind of
religion and it doesn't add up actually I think there are really good things about eating things
which are not remotely local for all sorts of reasons I mean first of all you know I grew up
at a time where you know the progressive view was always one of internationalism and connections
with other people and I think that part of the way we have food from all around the world is
part of that more cosmopolitan outward looking thing and I worry in Britain sometimes not many
mango trees in Glasgow, I can tell you. No, no, exactly. And so sometimes, you know, this sort of
like go local thing in Britain, what bothers me is it's happening as a cultural phenomenon about
the same sort of time where people are also talking about closing the borders, keeping the
immigrants out, etc. It's the benign side. It can be, not always. An element of it is a benign side
of actually a kind of a provincialism. But also on environmental grounds, it's not as straightforward
as local is better. Interesting reports done on New Zealand's products. New Zealand has lamb and
butter and everything. Now, they can produce it with a very low carbon footprint because they've
got the perfect environment from it. And internet shipping is a very, very low carbon way of
transferring things. The total carbon footprint of something grown in optimal conditions and shipped
very far distance can be less than something grown locally, where you have to put a lot of
synthetic inputs, artificial heating, greenhouses, and so forth. So I'm all for that, lots of getting
back in touch with the local and supporting it, and certainly avoiding foods which carry this
very, very heavy carbon footprint. But it's just too simplistic to think that everything that's
travelled a long way has a heavy carbon footprint. It doesn't. Bananas are great, you know? And bananas,
they don't grow here. We put them in ships, low carbon footprint, delicious, nutritious,
and even when fair trade, not very expensive. How do you think that looks when we have 10
billion people in 2050 and an estimated 28 billion by the end of the century? How do we
deal with those trade routes and shipping? And if we're still existing as we are now,
what are the implications for the planet? Well there have to be changes for various reasons
as one you pointed out but I think the solution for our food security is not to reduce our
interdependence. We're going to become more interdependent in a globalised world it's even
more important that we trade in ways that are efficient that we grow things where they grow
best and most efficiently and where we can transport them with a low carbon footprint we can.
If we try and grow everything local to us then what's going to happen is the people who are
blessed with the climates and everything they can do that will do well and other people are going to
starve, right? So we have to make these suggestions. Let's try this bit of moral calculus on you. So the
National Party in Australia, the country party, objects by and large to foreign interests buying
our farming land. Huge debate over very large livestock holding recently which the government
caved in on and said well they couldn't buy it in the way they were structured. And the theory here
is that, well, dairy produce, meat produce
is going to be grown and sent straight to China
and then we might be having a problem with food security.
What's the moral calculus around this?
Have the Chinese got a right to buy our agricultural land
and export directly to China in a growing world
which, if Damon's right,
we're going to need every scrap of food we can get?
Well, look, there are lots of issues tied up in that, right?
In terms of land ownership,
We have a system where people can privately own land, but it doesn't mean that once you've paid for it, it's yours and you can do what you like for it.
So it's really, without knowing the ins and outs of this particular debate, who owns it or not in a legal contract isn't really the key issue.
The main thing is there are regulations in any given country about how land is used, so it's used in a sustainable and fair way, and it benefits everybody, and it benefits the people here as well.
This debate has concerned me a little because I find sometimes it's a little racist.
It's always the Chinese.
And there are a lot of other foreign investors who are buying up Australian land and Australian
dairies and agricultural land.
So I'd like to see it just more about foreign interests rather than a particular nationality.
But I think this is the important thing about the education process about growing food is
that you see the importance of our food producers and our growers in the system.
And again, when you're an urban consumer going to the supermarket, you're not really thinking about where that food comes from, who's grown it, who's put all that effort into it.
And when you grow an eggplant and you understand the time, the effort, the commitment, the people who do that full time become your heroes.
And I think that this debate hopefully is repositioning our farmers in a better, more positive and strong light because without them, who is going to grow our food?
So we're seeing a dairy crisis as we speak?
We are. We are.
I mean, Julian sits on an organisation called the Food Ethics Council in the UK
and they talk about a square deal for farmers.
Do you think we're giving Australian farmers a square deal?
No, of course not.
I mean, we're seeing the death of our rural communities.
Farmers now are walking off the land.
We're seeing hugely high suicide rates amongst our farming community.
I think it's devastating.
I don't know how farmers are hanging in there,
but I think we need to bridge this urban and rural gap
that we've got at the moment
and I think food and understanding the importance of it
and how important that food is going to become for our future.
Australia is becoming more and more climate challenged.
We've only got a really thin, fertile strip
around the edge of our country to grow food
and the people who can do it well and do it productively
are really key to the future of our country.
Yeah, I think a symptom of that too
is that most people aren't aware
that I think 80 cents of every dollar that Australians spend
goes to either coals and woolies,
whether it's through food, alcohol, gambling, petrol.
So it's almost a dictatorship in a way.
And I think because of that impact,
the way they can affect the farmers there,
and I've met a farmer who grows lettuce,
and he said his quota that he has to provide every month
is 1,000 tonnes of lettuce.
Now, he has to grow that amount every single month.
But if a company only wants 400 tonnes,
then that 600 tonnes gets thrown out.
So the system is just so unproductive
the way we're doing it at the moment.
and this is where we need to rethink how we're approaching this.
And ultimately, it's probably a systemic problem that, as you said,
we've designed a system that...
But in the end, it's a market, and you've got to change the market
the way the market works.
So tell me how you would change...
But I think you've also got to help consumers make a much more informed question.
When a lot of consumers...
I worked at Choice, a consumer advocacy group,
and I was really fascinated by the main question that consumers ask themselves
when they go into a shop, how much does something cost?
That was their first question.
And if you talk to calls and willies, that's what they say.
It's price, price, price.
And obviously it's not always the best question.
And so what I hope we can help people do is ask the other questions they need to ask.
Why does it cost that?
Why doesn't it cost this?
Who's made it?
What's gone into it?
How's it been produced?
How are those animals being treated?
There are a whole lot of other questions.
I mean, when you get a litre of milk the same or cheaper than a litre of water,
you know something's gone wrong.
As a consumer, you shouldn't go, yeah, that's fantastic.
You should say, someone's being screwed over here.
And it's the water buyers.
So, Damon, how do you square your view about food miles with, if you like, social justice across nations,
where coffee producers, cocoa producers, and increasingly others,
as sub-Saharan Africa gets a bit richer, they'll start producing grain and other things, drought allowing.
don't they have a right to sell their products on an international market
and ship them to distant places?
Of course, and I think what we're losing here is that we're switching to extremities.
We're not saying that suddenly we stop all trade and shipping.
If there are certain things that still require that
and they are available at a certain price because they're a special...
Yeah, absolutely.
But like I said, when we're shipping apples between countries
for no reason other than the polishing,
I think there's a broken system there
because it's cheaper to do that for them than do it within their own country.
That's the issue we need to address.
What I'm losing here in this discussion is, if you like, I'm sorry, being boring and practical,
how you adjust the market so that it's different for apples from coffee.
Look, it is really, really difficult. I think this is true.
Now, the thing about the market system, the so-called perfection of the market,
is there is a lot of kind of truth involved in it, right?
One reason why it's good to have trade is that it's more efficient for some people to do a lot of one thing
rather than everyone to do everything themselves.
An apple tree in every garden is not as efficient as an orchard from which we all take things.
So there's no simple answer to this.
And food is also complicated because supply is not easily switched on and off
because there are all sorts of things to do with the weather and the seasons this year and everything.
So, you know, getting it perfectly right is very difficult.
But I think the point is you shouldn't be seduced by the idea of what will the perfect system look like.
I think we can see lots of examples already where systems have emerged for various usually political reasons,
which just have bizarre and perverse consequences.
And I think it's a...
Such as?
Subsidies, for example, for grain.
I mean, it's particularly bad in America.
America subsidises the production of certain crops.
Fructose is the classic one.
Yeah, exactly, which creates this glut of fructose,
which means it has to be put into everything,
and corn syrup and everything.
So there are lots of perverse incentives there.
And there's also not the right kind of taxation.
You know, we put taxation on things,
and, you know, we have very crude categories for this.
You know, luxury goods get sales taxed in the UK,
basic foodstuffs don't,
but what fits into what category varies.
So, you know, I think, in a way,
There's nothing really simple and inspiring that we can say about this.
We have to go ad hoc, bit by bit, changing this bit of regulation, that regulation,
trying to nudge ourselves towards something.
And also having the humility to realise that this is a bit experimental.
Markets and food supply systems are extremely complicated
and there's always the risk of unintentionally having a perverse outcome.
